https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/30/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter: Ha valaki egy neki nem tetsző személyi döntés miatt eltávolodik a Tiszától, ehhez is szíve joga van Belföld Bakró-Nagy Ferenc Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hosszú bejegyzésben sorolta Magyar Péter a Tisza-kormány eddigi eredményeit, majd rátért a kritikus pontra, a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal vezetőinek kinevezésére. Azt írja, hogy teljesítették az egyik legfőbb vállalásukat, rekord idő alatt létrehozva „Európa talán legerősebb korrupcióellenes intézményét” (ehhez egyelőre az elnököt és a négyből egy elnökhelyettest neveztek ki, a hivatal felállítása csak ezután kezdődik). „Szeretném újra világossá tenni, hogy soha nem vállaltunk olyat (és más kormány sem vállal ilyet), hogy minden vezetői pozícióra meg fogjuk a közvéleménnyel szavaztatni a jelölteket” – írta. Ezt azzal indokolta, hogy nem a közvélemény és az állampolgárok felelőssége, hogy ki az adott pozícióra a legmegfelelőbb jelölt, hanem azé, aki kinevezi. A miniszterelnök „érzi”, hogy a demokrácia újratanulásában „lesznek döccenők, akár néha személyes csalódások is”, de a személyek kinevezéséért a megválasztott vezető a felelős, „nem egy influenszer, nem egy volt politikus és nem is a közvélemény többsége. Ha mindig a közvélemény döntene kinevezésekről, jogszabályokról, költségvetésről, adókról, akkor az ország kormányozhatatlanná válna.” Ezután védelmébe vette a képviselőit, akik szerinte mindent a hazájuknak rendeltek alá, és minden döntést ennek tudatában hoznak meg, akkor is, ha az adott pillanatban ez nem tűnik népszerűnek. „Lehet ezért minket kritizálni, lehet velünk egyet nem érteni” – ismételte meg a többször megfogalmazott állítást, hozzátéve, hogy a lelkiismeretük tiszta, nálunk jobban senki nem szeretné az elsíbolt állami vagyonok visszaszerzését és a felelősök megbüntetését. Végül ismét a tiszás közösségnek üzent, a péntekinél egy fokkal keményebben: „Természetesen ha valaki a 110 napos kormányzásunk eredményei mellett egy neki nem tetsző személyi döntés miatt eltávolodik a Tiszától, ehhez is szíve joga van” – írta. Majd hozzátette, hogy ők semmilyen nyomásra nem fognak engedni a vállalásaikból, és pontot tett az ügy végére: „Részemről a kérdés a fentiek szerint lezárva”. Pénteken a hivatal elnöke a Telex stúdiójában járt, megválasztása után először a Telexnek adott videós interjút. „Tudom, hogy mindenki az elszámoltatást várja, tudom, hogy mindenki a bilincsek kattanását várja, és tudom, hogy mindenki szeretné hallani a zörgő rácsokat, de létre kell hozni a hivatalt, meg kell választani még három elnökhelyettest” – mondta Unger Anna, akit pénteken titkos szavazáson választott meg az Országgyűlés a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal (NVVH) élére. Unger azt ígérte, a következő hetekben azon lesz, hogy megtalálja a legjobb munkatársakat az elnökhelyettesekkel együttműködve minden lehetséges pozícióra. "To be frank, it should that our concept to minimize the results of the AfD did not work out yet," he said. https://english.elpais.com/international.text: Russia is stepping up its hybrid war against Europe. From sabotage, drone incursions, and arson to plots (mostly foiled) to assassinate pro‑Ukraine activists and Russian dissidents on European soil, the Kremlin is testing the allied response, and incidents against NATO’s European partners are becoming more serious, such as the explosive‑laden drones found this summer at Leipzig Airport in Germany. That gray line between a hybrid attack and a conventional one is blurring, and several European intelligence sources warn of the risk that one of those incidents could escalate — either by a deliberate Kremlin decision or a miscalculation. “What would have happened if the explosives at Leipzig Airport had detonated?” asks a senior EU source. Senior European and NATO officials consulted over the past week share the concern — not because of a conventional military assault but because that gray boundary is becoming ever more fragile. “The greatest danger now is that the hybrid war will accidentally cross a red line,” says another veteran source, who points to an incident two weeks ago in which flares were fired from a Russian frigate at a Danish helicopter as an example. In fact, Emily Ferris, a researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), says the serious episode involving explosive drones in Leipzig — which Germany clearly attributed to the Kremlin on September 1 — “showed that Moscow, and probably NATO itself, still lacks clarity on the current red lines that would trigger a military response.” The Kremlin is furious at the stalemate in its war against Ukraine — which is approaching its fifth anniversary — and is moving to undermine allied support for Kyiv while testing the West’s response capacity, which so far has been relatively mild. The uptick in attacks is also occurring at an especially vulnerable moment for Europe, as it considers how to operate without the security umbrella of the United States and on the eve of a key super election year for the European project. In recent weeks the alarm has risen sharply and Europe is beginning to bunker down against a threat that is becoming less and less hybrid. “We are preparing to face and survive a new kind of war,” admits a European intelligence source. One that does not necessarily involve missiles or tanks but could paralyze a country and undermine society through cuts to water and energy supplies, disruptions to computer systems, or weeks‑long closures of its airports, the source stresses. Temperatures are rising in European capitals and the secret visit by CIA director John Ratcliffe to Moscow on August 25, the mystery over its purpose, and the messages he received there, has fed concern. The trip revived an unsettling precedent: the last time a CIA director traveled to Moscow was in November 2021, when William Burns tried to dissuade the Kremlin from invading Ukraine. Vladimir Putin launched the full‑scale war on February 24, 2022. As such, Keir Giles, a researcher at the Chatham House think tank, says the comparison is inevitable — and the parallel, he adds, shows how seriously the U.S. appears to view the current Russian threats. Russia is multiplying its hostile and criminal acts, French President Emmanuel Macron warned a few days ago, saying the nature of the Russian aggression and those threats in Europe is changing. It is intensifying. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he has intelligence indicating the Kremlin is preparing to escalate hybrid attacks by late autumn and winter, coinciding with a particularly “critical” moment on the battlefield in Ukraine. Danish intelligence services warned last week that there is a risk Russia could carry out a “limited” attack on one or more NATO member states in the coming months. However, despite the alarms — especially from the Baltic and Nordic countries, which are closest to Russia and the most direct and frequent victims of these incidents — no ally has invoked NATO’s Article 4, which states member countries “will consult together whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened,” military sources note. The Atlantic Alliance is deliberately ambiguous about its response to this and other types of threats. Last week, its secretary-general, Mark Rutte, warned that the Russian menace will remain for the long term and urged Kyiv’s allies to “stay calm, carry on, and keep supporting Ukraine.” “Russia, in the end, is doing this because they are not successful at the moment in Ukraine,” he insisted during his visit to the United States in a conversation with that country’s ambassador to NATO, Matthew G. Whitaker. The U.S. representative was blunt. “The first shot of any future global conflict is not going to be troops across a border. It is going to be attacks on infrastructure and attacks on technology and very sophisticated increasing hybrid warfare,” Whitaker said, calling for preparation not only for conventional war but also for hybrid war. “We’re going to have to do it all at the same time,” he warned. Europe and its outlook have shifted a great deal over the last year. “Hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her solemn state of the Union speech to the European Parliament on September 16. Brussels is finalizing a security strategy that aims to strengthen strategic capabilities — air and missile defense, transport, space, and cybersecurity — create a common response framework to hybrid threats, and an emergency protocol that would allow the 27 to coordinate when an incident seriously threatens a member state without constituting an armed attack, EU sources explain. That strategy complements preparedness plans — which design measures so the population can be self‑sufficient for at least 72 hours in any emergency, from climate to armed conflict — and other infrastructure reinforcement plans. Von der Leyen, a strong Atlanticist, stresses that NATO will remain the pillar of collective defense, but she has also spoken of creating a kind of “Article 4” modeled on NATO’s that would adapt current institutions and decision‑making mechanisms — designed for a “different world” — to today’s situation, the head of the EU executive said. Yet nobody in Brussels seems very clear on what that mechanism will look like or what it will entail. Thus, the European Union — the institutions and its member states — is constructing, piece by piece, a new security architecture for a continent that can no longer clearly separate peace from confrontation. France is finalizing a special plan to protect critical infrastructure and the most sensitive facilities of its defense industry against drones and Russian cyberattacks. The Netherlands is stepping up its civil preparedness plans. Denmark has activated a “total defense” plan and mobilized €161 million to strengthen water and electricity supplies, telecommunications, hospitals and transport. Sweden has announced a new €1.3 billion package for its air defense and is preparing, together with its neighbors, civilian evacuation plans. Norway has declared 2026 the “year of total defense.” Poland has tightened protection of its infrastructure. Lithuania is fortifying its strategic facilities against drones and sabotage. Belgium has launched its first national defense plan since the Cold War. The Kremlin and its intelligence services declared a hybrid war on Europe long ago. Sabotage and targeted killings on European soil are part of the hallmark of its intelligence agencies. In 2018, officers from Russia’s military intelligence service (GRU) attacked their own former agent Sergei Skripal in the United Kingdom; a year later, in a Berlin park, a Russian citizen murdered Chechen exile Zelimkhan Khangoshvili on orders from “Russia’s central directorate,” according to the Higher Regional Court in Berlin. Now, despite the blow to Russian espionage in the early stages of the Ukraine war (with thousands of expulsions of alleged diplomats and officers posted in Europe), such attacks are more frequent. And more serious. A study by the U.S. think tank the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which has compiled its own database, says Russian sabotage — cutting submarine cables, GPS interference, attacks on defense companies — has increased since 2024. In addition, intelligence officials cited by the Associated Press say Russia’s campaign of targeted killings in Europe has not only grown since the invasion but has also expanded its targets. They are no longer just deserters (such as Maxim Kuzminov, the Russian helicopter pilot who switched to the Ukrainian side before going into exile in Spain, where he was murdered in 2024) or former agents; they now include Russian opponents and foreigners who support Ukraine. Lithuania’s prosecutor’s office points to Russia, and particularly the GRU, as responsible for a foiled plot last year to assassinate Russian‑Bashkir dissident Ruslan Gabbasov and Lithuanian activist Valdas Bartkevičius. For decades, Europe could think of war as something that happened beyond its borders. Today the situation is different. It has stopped treating its rear areas as a safe, separate zone from the front and now sees them as spaces vulnerable to sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage, and strikes on critical infrastructure with grave consequences. https://www.courant.com/2026/10/04/from-.text: Henrietta Ustjanauskas and her son, Alexander Phibbs, show photos and documents of Anthony and Ada Ustjanauskas displayed at Henrietta’s home in Simsbury on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) By Livi Stanford | lstanford@courant.com | Hartford Courant staff PUBLISHED: October 4, 2026 at 5:19 AM EDT | UPDATED: October 4, 2026 at 11:58 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... When a 19-year-old Lithuanian Holocaust survivor walked into the courtroom for the May 1946 Nuremberg Trials, several Nazis turned their heads to see her, her burnt orange dress a stark contrast to the drab uniforms in the room. Ada Gens-Ustjanauskus had escaped with her Catholic mother, Elvyra, from an area in proximity to the Vilna ghetto in 1945, then traveled with other survivors associated with the Ex-Concentration Camp Orchestra. The group later invited her to Nuremberg, where she observed the International Military Tribunal’s prosecution of Nazi war criminals over two days. Gens-Ustjanauskas, a former West Hartford resident now known for decades of work aiding immigrants and running an international grocery store, reflected on the trial with her family as this week marks the 80th anniversary of Nuremberg, which established the first international criminal tribunals to hold those in government accountable for atrocities. “I think justice was done,” said Gens-Ustjanauskas in testimony to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, referring to Nuremberg. “I saw the criminal element who ruined my life, who ruined my mother’s life, who killed my father, who killed millions of people, and that is what I thought.” In total, “199 defendants were tried at Nuremberg, 161 were convicted, and 37 were sentenced to death, including 12 tried by the IMT, including Hermann Goring, Hitler’s right-hand man,” according to the Holocaust museum. Observing a trial of personal significance, Gens-Ustjanauskas saw second-ranking American prosecutor Thomas J. Dodd, who more than a decade later became a Connecticut senator and would forge a path with the Holocaust survivor’s family to support the independence of the Baltic states in northeastern Europe, including Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, which were under Soviet control. In 1965, Dodd issued a resolution calling for the restoration of freedom to the Baltic states. The Ustjanauskas family held political rallies also calling for independence and established four parcel agencies allowing immigrants in the United States to send clothing, food, and other goods to those living under Soviet rule. Facing the perpetrators who were among those responsible for killing 6 million Jews struck the nearly 100-year-old Holocaust survivor as she confronted her own grief of the loss of family members, including her father Jacob Gens. Gens, a complex figure in Holocaust history, had served as the Jewish chief of police in the Vilna ghetto, an area designated specifically for Jews in Lithuania during World War II, and was tasked with the unthinkable role of deciding which Jews to turn over to the Nazis. Following accusations that he was aiding partisan groups, he was ordered to return to the Gestapo, where he was murdered in 1943. The court proceedings lasted nearly a year, from November 1945 to October 1946, in Nuremberg, the city where the race laws of 1935 were established, which led to the Holocaust. Former Senator Christopher Dodd told the Courant that his father believed in the merits of the international court. Quoting one of the many letters his father sent to his wife, Grace Murphy Dodd, which the former senator published in a book, Thomas Dodd said, “I’ll never do anything as important again in my life.” Christopher Dodd said it was remarkable to bring together different legal systems from France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States in a trial where there was “no bickering over whose criminal system is better.” In his final argument on Aug. 29, 1946, Thomas Dodd struggled with the magnitude of the atrocities. “We simply cannot comprehend six million murders,” he told the tribunal. James Waller, Gladstein family distinguished chair in human rights at UConn, at the Gladstein Human Rights Center, which houses the historical Thomas J. Dodd papers, said the birth of the institute is traced to Dodd’s papers and the legacy of Nuremberg. The papers consist of interrogation notes, reports on concentration camps, documents on forced labor policies and information on the concentration camp system, among others, according to information from the Office of Legislative Research. Waller said one of the lessons of Nuremberg is that “impunity cannot win. “Perpetrators and would-be perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity have to recognize that one day justice will be done,” Waller said. After her father’s death, Gens-Ustjanauskas was forced into hiding with her mother, surviving in the Lithuanian countryside. In 1945, she escaped to Poland and then to Germany, according to her grandson Alexander Phibbs. Phibbs founded the Gens Family Project in honor of his grandmother and to recover the people, places and stories left behind in Jewish Lithuania, which was destroyed in the Holocaust and the continued occupation of the Soviet Union. Terrified of Stalin and reflections on Nuremberg Photos and documents of Anthony Ustjanauskas with U.S. Sen. Thomas J. Dodd are displayed at his daughter’s home in Simsbury on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) Thomas Dodd shared misgivings about the Soviet forced labor camps during Stalin’s leadership and that the Soviet Union was part of the four allies at Nuremberg. “Everything that we have charged the Germans with in this case has been done, and worse, is being done by Russia,” said Thomas Dodd during the Nuremberg trials. Later, in the congressional record of Feb. 23, 1965, Thomas Dodd said that, “If one accepts the average population of the slave labor camps as 10 million over the 20 odd years of Joseph Stalin’s undisputed rule, this would mean that approximately 2 million slave laborers died annually in Stalin’s camps, or 40 million for the 20-year period.” During the same interview, Gens-Ustjanauskas was asked whether she thought the Nuremberg trials were victor’s justice because the Soviet Union was involved. In response, Gens-Ustjanauskas said the crimes committed by the Soviet Union came to light later and that this was not at the forefront of her mind during the trial. Watching the trials, Gens-Ustjanauskas recalled how Albert Speer, Hitler’s chief architect, when asked whether he knew about the concentration camps, said ‘no.’ “And then they opened a big screen and you could see golden frames of eyeglasses, golden teeth and golden jewelry and they said, ‘How do you think Mr. Speer, your treasury got all this stuff without you knowing where it came from?” Speer did not have an answer, she said. “So that registered in my mind,” she said. “It was so impressive.” While observing the trials at Nuremberg, Gens-Ustjanauskas also had to stay clear of the Soviets, which made it more terrifying, according to her daughter, Henrietta Phibbs. Through all of it, Henrietta Phibbs said her mother never lost her optimism, a gift she learned from her father. It was her mother’s optimism that helped keep her and her family safe after the war, Henrietta Phibbs said. Dodd and the Ustjanauskas family were deeply impacted by the evil they saw before them in the Nuremberg trials, and it impacted how they moved forward in the world. Thomas Dodd later became a senator, and in 1968 he introduced several gun control bills, including “strict control over the sale of ammunition and the registration of all firearms,” which failed to make it into the final provisions of the omnibus crime bill, according to UConn archives. Dodd also continued to advocate for independence for the Baltic States. In 1967, he faced trouble when the “Senate investigated allegations that he had diverted public funds for personal use,” according to UConn archives. He was censured in 1968. Gens-Ustjanauskas went on to help thousands of immigrants navigate complex immigration systems, assisting USCIS and other federal agencies, the Gens Family Project said. She traveled internationally with American presidents and vice presidents to Lithuania and the Baltic states. She and her husband, Antanas Ustjanauskas, opened an international food store and parcel agency now known as Cosmos, which closed in 2022 after 65 years in business. The two families’ lives intersected once again in their dedication to fight for independence for the Baltic states in the early 1960s. A connection made through a fight for independence A photo of Ada Ustjanauskas with Lithuanian delegates and other memorabilia from her past are displayed at her daughter’s home in Simsbury on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) Ada and Antanas Ustjanauskas connected with Sen. Thomas Dodd after Nuremberg in their work to send goods to people under Soviet rule. Antanas encountered an issue when he complained to Dodd in November 1961 that 8,000 parcels sent from Hartford were rejected by the Soviet Union for nonpayment of customs duties and shipped back to New York, according to Courant archives. The senator called for an investigation leading to a federal grand jury charging the General Parcel and Travel Company, the shipping organization responsible for the handling of the packages, with 16 counts of mail fraud in the disappearance of thousands of dollars in Russian custom duties, according to Courant archives. The families’ friendship continued when the Ustjanauskas family founded the Hundred Club of Connecticut in 1967 to support the families of police officers and others killed in the line of duty. Alexander Phibbs said Thomas Dodd, who served as a senator from 1959 to 1970, became a strong supporter of the organization and one of its first members. Christopher Dodd said to this day people stop him concerning his father’s work in fighting for independence from the Baltic States. “He was very active on these issues, and to this day people from the captive nations held very strongly that we weren’t tough enough,” he said. “There were a lot of people, well-intended, who said we shouldn’t bother being critical of the Soviet Union in those days because they helped us win the war. And it made my father furious.” Reflecting on family legacies Decades after the war, Gens-Ustjanauskas went on to work with the U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Special Investigations, particularly with Nazi perpetrators who had made new lives in the states, Henrietta Phibbs said. “So she’s sitting next to these people, and they loved her,” Henrietta Phibbs said. “They confided in her. They were telling her things they weren’t going to tell the government. And she used to come home and tell us she’s sitting next to these murderers. They don’t know who she is and she is certainly not going to tell them.” In 1990, Gens-Ustjanauskas provided interpretation for President George W. Bush while meeting with Lithuanian Chairman Vytautas Landsbergis. In 1992, in celebration of Lithuania’s restored freedom, Gens-Ustjanauskas translated Vice President Dan Quayle’s address. “After living through one of the most tragic periods in modern history, and losing both her family and her homeland, Ada dedicated the rest of her life to helping others who found themselves in a similar position,” said Alexander Phibbs. “She believed that giving back to her community was her duty as a human being.” Henrietta Phibbs said she respected how her mother, in spite of everything she went through, never said a bad thing about another person and focused on helping others, including hundreds of immigrants. Even during the Holocaust, Henrietta said her mother would run errands for people in the ghetto, risking the Germans seeing her. She ended up conducting so many errands that she needed surgery on her foot, Henrietta Phibbs said. She said that mindset has impacted her own family’s life in focusing on helping those in need, including forming a nonprofit at one time to provide programs for children in the summer, she said. Christopher Dodd said he was proud of his father for his work at Nuremberg. “I admired him for his guts and courage to stand up for things he believed in very deeply,” he said while also acknowledging the challenges of his father’s censure, which he said deeply pained him when he died six months later. Dodd said he appreciated how his father focused on the emphasis of the rule of law in the Nuremberg trials compared to the vision of others like Winston Churchill, who believed that the Nazis should just be shot. “My father often felt that there had been an international criminal justice system after the end of World War I,” he said. “He used to say maybe that might have been enough to convince the Nazi leadership that they better be careful what they did because there would be a judgment on them after the war. And that wasn’t the case considering how we’ve never supported the International Criminal Court. My father was a huge advocate.” He said his father fought for the genocide convention’s adoption. Alexander Phibbs said Thomas Dodd was a shining example of “the humanity of the U.S. government” and Christopher Dodd said Ada’s story touched him. Reflecting on the 80th anniversary of Nuremberg, Gens-Ustjanauskas said, “The world couldn’t understand how the Nazis could kill so many people. “Nuremberg exposed the mindset of individuals who murdered millions and then claimed innocence,” she said. “Finding them guilty of war crimes against humanity was a warning to those who find the murder of citizens a solution to their own problems.” Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Most Popular Most Popular CT restaurant closes due to ‘unexpected and unavoidable challenges’ CT restaurant closes due to 'unexpected and unavoidable challenges' 223-unit residential development proposed for tiny CT town. The artifact in question is part of a bronze ring used like a keychain to hold strigils, curved metal instruments used by bathers to scrape oil and dirt off their skin. Two figures decorating the ring enact a bizarre scene in which a person seems to subdue a large bird with a knife. After conducting a 3D scan of the artifact, Mustață determined that the figures are combatants in an eternal struggle between pygmies and migrating cranes recounted in the Iliad . This bit of Homeric comic relief served as a set piece in Greek and Roman artwork for centuries. The pygmy on the ring, however, departs from other depictions of the myth, which tend to emphasize the pygmies’ playfulness. “This might be the most serious pygmy in all of ancient Roman art,” Mustață says. “One can detect a sense of satisfaction on his face as he glances at the viewer.” She notes that the pygmy’s victorious pose resembles depictions of Hercules defeating the Nemean lion, the first of the hero’s twelve labors. Somewhat undermining this triumphant moment is an oversize representation of the pygmy’s feces. “We may have a pygmy attempting to assume the heroic posture of Hercules,” says Mustață, “while at the same time being so frightened that he can’t control his bodily functions.” Whoever made the ring was, it seems, putting their own twist on an already ancient gag.
